title: As immigration arrests surge, advocates rue lawmakers’ failure to pass protections in 2025
summary: A proposal to ban 287(g) agreements -- which allow local police to cooperate with, and in some cases act in place of, federal immigration agents -- failed at the last-minute in the 2025 General Assembly, but it could be a major topic in 2026.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 30, 2025

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters December 30, 2025

George Escobar doesn’t like to use the phrase “told you so,” but after seeing a surge in immigration arrests that advocates had warned about when lawmakers failed to pass limits on local immigration enforcement, it’s hard to avoid.

Escobar, the incoming executive director of the immigrant advocacy group CASA, was referring to last-minute action in the Maryland Senate during the 2025 General Assembly that stripped out a proposal to ban “287(g)” agreements, which allow local police agencies to work with federal immigration officials. Eight counties in Maryland have signed such agreements, five of them just this year.

Passing that bill is “our No. 1 priority for the legislative session,” said Escobar, who takes over at CASA on Jan. 1. Del. Nicole Williams (D-Prince George’s), the lead sponsor on last session’s bill, has vowed to bring it back in the 2026 General Assembly, and the proposal has gained a powerful new supporter since last spring in Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), who said he supports the bill.

“It is frustrating thinking about the obstacles that we faced and the evidence that we shared,” Escobar earlier said this month. “We have seen changes even in our legislators like our Senate president. We always welcome a change of heart, and that support will mean the difference between life and death.”

To Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins, a longtime defender of 287(g) agreements, that sort of talk is just political hype from opponents of a program he said has worked well since his county joined in 2008.

“I will argue any day of the week, with anybody that the fact we have removed 1,877 criminals out of this county, not to reoffend, not to commit more crimes, we are a safe county because of it,” Jenkins said.

The debate comes as immigration detentions in Maryland, as in the rest of the country, have surged in the past year under President Donald Trump. Data from the Prison Policy Initiative showed the more than 3,000 people in Maryland were arrested this year by Immigration and Customs Enforcement: 1,193 from Jan. 20, when Trump was inaugurated, through May 20, and another 1,940 from May 21 to Oct. 15.

The 287(g) program was first established in 1996, but it has gained more attention, and more scrutiny, since Trump returned to office. Versions of the program include allowing local officials to execute administrative immigration warrants in their jails, identifying and beginning removal proceedings against individuals arrested by local law enforcement, and serving on task forces that officers “enforce limited immigration authority.”

Five sheriff’s departments in Maryland – Allegany, Carroll, Garrett, St. Mary’s and Washington counties – signed 287(g) this year. Frederick, Cecil and Harford counties already had agreements in place. All the Maryland agreements are limited to the counties’ jails: If a local department determines that someone they arrested is undocumented, it will hold that inmate for an additional 48 hours for ICE to come get them

Still, advocates said the program incentives racial profiling, especially of Latinos.

Williams said she sponsored the Maryland Values Act — and plans to do so again next year — because it’s just the right thing to do. If Maryland banned 287(g) agreements it would be following the lead of several other states, she said. Those states include Illinois, California and New Jersey.

“Contrary to what some may say, I think it [287(g) program] does more harm from a public safety standpoint than a benefit,” Williams said. “It has a very chilling effect on individuals within our communities all across the state from wanting to engage and participate with law enforcement

“This is about ensuring all of our communities, regardless of where you live in the state … that they know that law enforcement is there for everyone and not just certain individuals within our state,” she said.

But Jenkins said he does not think a ban would be constitutional, and that it would be certain to draw a legal challenge.

“I’m not a lawyer, but I don’t believe they have the authority as a legislature to take away my authority to make a decision to enter into an agreement to keep my county safe. I think there’s a [legal] challenge there,” he said.

He disagrees with those who say the agreement encourages racial profiling. While the agreement allows the sheriff’s department to ask a person’s citizenship or immigration status, that is only after they have been arrested on another charge, he said.

“It has nothing to do with race or ethnicity. It has nothing to do with going after people,” Jenkins said. “Everything we do in this program is after the physical arrest. I have to put you in handcuffs and take you to jail.

“All this fear is political hype,” he said. “I think it’s largely political rhetoric by the people who don’t want any enforcement whatsoever.”

But Escobar pointed to a 2008 case in Frederick County, when a woman successfully sued the county after sheriff’s deputies arrested her on a civil immigration warrant while she was eating her lunch on a park bench before work. According to a summary of the case, Roxana Orellana Santos was held in the county jail before being turned over to ICE, where she was held for 46 days, away from her then 1-year-old U.S. child,

“You fast-forward to today and the same thing is happening,” Escobar said.

Critics of the program invoke the case of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran immigrant who was stopped by federal agents, detained and almost immediately deported. His case has become a high-profile example of Trump administration deportation policies.

Strictly, Abrego Garcia’s case has nothing to do with 287(g), since it was carried out solely by federal authorities. But critics of the program say it opens the door to the types of stops and detention that ensnared Abrego Garcia.

“It’s time for the Maryland General Assembly to step it up and eliminate 287(g) because we want to be a state that is based on community trust and eliminating 287(g) is part of that goal,” said Montgomery County Council president Natali Fani-González, who has participated in rallies in support of Abrego Garcia.

Darren Popkin, executive director of the Maryland Sheriffs’ Association, said his organization will not take a position on Williams’ bill until seeing a draft of the legislation.

But at a hearing earlier this year on House Bill 1222, Popkin wrote in a March 27 letter with the Maryland Chiefs of Police Association htat they opposed the measure.

“HB 1222 … imposes a one-size-fits-all mandate that strips local jurisdictions of their ability to make determinations that best serve the safety and well-being of their communities,” the letter said.

Popkin reiterated that point in an interview this month.

“The sheriffs and the public in those jurisdictions have made policy decisions that they believe keep their communities safer to have these programs within their detention centers, which limits the immigration activities outside of the detention centers,” he said, adding that it “is not accurate” to suggest that local sheriffs are performing immigration enforcement in their communities under the agreements.

Still, Escobar said local governments should not work with “paramilitary forces” like ICE.

“We’re talking about voluntary agreements that these sheriffs are engaging in [with] the federal government to help them do their job,” he said. “It is fundamentally damaging local law enforcement’s relationship with the community.”
